In his October 9th article titled Three ways to cure the disenchanted he states

Indeed, if you vote for anyone in any seat other than the winning party, you might as well not bother: your vote will have no impact on the result.

It goes (IMO) deeper than that. Unless your vote is for the party leader who gathered the greatest minority of votes for his/her party your vote has little or no impact on what government will do during its mandate.

In a rare moment of honesty Stephen Harper once said (letter to the The National Post, February of 1998)

“Let's face it, the average backbench MP is little more than a bench warmer for his/her political party.”

The other parties, except for the Green party, dance around it but if they were equally honest they would admit the same. Rank and file MPs may wear the mantle of 'representative for their riding' but in reality are simple proxy votes for their party leader - regardless of what they may think going into the election their primary role is not representing their constituency, it is to represent the will of their party leader in the House of Commons by voting how and when they are told to do so, and (of course) by reciting on demand the party talking points handed to them as they walk through the doors.

Our "democracy" has, in a majority government scenario, developed into something as close to one person rule as it can without changing its name to something else that would more honestly describe what it is.

So how do we change that? Coyne suggests that proportional representation would make each vote count, and I agree that it would, with an added side benefit. Proportional representation would also make majority governments harder to achieve, and that would transfer some of the power party leaders have gathered into their offices back to the MPs in their caucus. If you form the government by a five seat count then you have to make damn sure that all of your MPs are behind you; and you certainly can't afford to banish or sanction any of your caucus for failure to follow orders.

As I have previously said in this space, my ideal result coming out of this election is an NDP [slim] minority that holds power only by the grace of the Liberals (and maybe a few Red Tories). It's a situation that not only moves the maximum amount of power pack into the hands of MPs themselves but limits the ability of the party in power to ram whatever legislation it wants through The House via the power of the Party Whip.

And that is as close to real democracy as we can probably hope for.
